title: I've spent years developing a machine learning model for Bitcoin direction prediction. Here's what I've learned.
author: Public_Luck_4753
selftext:
​

I've been working on a machine learning-based Bitcoin prediction system for quite some time.

The objective was relatively simple: instead of predicting an exact Bitcoin price, I wanted to estimate the probability of its direction over the next five days.

**A few things I focused on:**

\* Using historical OHLCV market data.

\* Treating the problem as a classification task rather than regression.

\* Evaluating directional predictions instead of exact price targets.

\* Testing the model against historical market conditions.

\* Evaluating its behaviour with live market data.

One thing I learned is that getting a model to perform well on historical data is only one part of the problem. Understanding how it behaves on unseen and changing market conditions is much more important.

I'm interested in discussing how others approach machine learning for financial time-series prediction.

**For those working on similar problems:**

1. Do you prefer classification or regression for directional trading strategies?

2. How do you deal with changing market regimes?

3. What validation methods have worked best for your financial ML projects?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Classification for direction makes sense, since you mostly care about the call and its probability. With a five-day target, check that your train and test periods don't overlap, because neighbouring days share most of the same future and can leak into each other. I'd also compare against a dumb baseline like "always up" and test in time order, rolling forward, not shuffled. Cymetica's Backtest Labs can hold the last 30% of history aside as out-of-sample, which is a simple extra check.
